extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate coffee-house readers; general readers of The Tatler (interested in social commentary, literary advice, and morals)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, epistolary/essay pieces of social commentary and literary criticism (as in Steele's Tatler), offering practical advice on manners, writing, and moral judgement for a cultured public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal your meaning in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "to write without discovering your meaning, bears a just resemblance to marching without beat of drum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should make the author's meaning clear and suited to the occasion; avoid producing work that hides its purpose or intention. (Context: the remark accompanies praise of a poem 'admirably suited to the occasion.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: express sorrow from actors, not observers
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the common fault ... that you give us rather the sentiments of such who behold tragical events, than of such who bear a part in them themselves. ... The way of common writers in this kind, is rather the description, than the expression of sorrow. There is no medium in these attempts; and you must go to the very bottom of the heart, or it is all mere language; and the writer of such lines is no more a poet, than a man is a physician for knowing the names of distempers, without the causes of them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice for writing tragedy: portray inward feeling and authentic, first-person suffering rather than secondhand description; aim for profound emotional truth ('the very bottom of the heart') or else the result is empty rhetoric. Read Shakespeare closely as a model (example: Morton's speech in 2 Henry IV demonstrates the noble, inward expression of grief). If a writer cannot genuinely feel the sorrow, postpone or choose less heroic subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial empathy when depicting great men
rubrics_metrics.description: "he who describes the concern of great men, must have a soul as noble, and as susceptible of high thoughts, as they whom he represents."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a writer lacks the inner stature or sensibility of the figures he attempts to portray (e.g., heroes), his drama will not ring true; better to 'lay by' such grand drama and write about more modest, believable cares and griefs suited to the author's capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose advisers with direct experience
rubrics_metrics.description: "you are not to choose your physician for his knowledge in your distemper, but for having it himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking counsel (medical or metaphorical), prefer advisers who have firsthand experience of the condition. (Anecdote: the narrator cured Tom Spindle's 'spleen' by using poetry because the physician could not empathise — the narrator's remedy relied on shared sensibility.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle fops/coxcombs by ridicule or genial reception, not stern contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be much more easy therefore to laugh him into reason, than convert him from his foppery by any serious contempt. ... People that want sense, do always in an egregious manner want modesty, which made our hero triumph in making his amour as public as was possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical social tactic: rather than attempting to mortify or angrily rebuke a vain fool, use laughter, light ridicule, or genial reception to deflate his pretensions. Examples given in the Tunbridge/Sir Taffety story: public mockery, persistent sociability, or gentle derision are more effective than harsh scorn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish love from lust in depiction and moral judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is a beauteous blind child ... to intimate ... that the person beloved has no intention to give us the anxieties we meet with; but that the beauties of a worthy object are like the charms of a lovely infant. On the other side ... Lust in the form of a satyr ... to signify, that the followers of it prostitute the reason of a man to pursue the appetites of a beast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing relationships and evaluating characters, treat 'love' as ennobling, innocent, and imitative of virtue (example: Aspasia; Florio & Amanda), and treat 'lust' as base, jealous, and destructive (example: Limberham & Corinna; Messalina). Use these archetypes to show moral consequences and to shape character behaviour believably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate public reputation by underlying conscience, not mere appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Among these men, honour and credit are not valuable possessions in themselves, or pursued out of a principle of justice; but merely as they are serviceable to ambition and to commerce. ... The world will never be in any manner of order or tranquillity, till men are firmly convinced, that conscience, honour, and credit, are all in one interest; and that without the concurrence of the former, the latter are but impositions upon ourselves and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social critique: distinguish between superficial credit/honour (performance for reputation) and genuine moral conscience. In evaluating individuals or institutions (e.g., merchants, courtiers), privilege integrity (conscience) as the true measure of honour and credit; beware systems that value appearance over ethical substance. Illustrated via personified figures Alethes (conscience), Verisimilis (honour/appearance), and Umbra (credit).
